text.text: Does the target of speech shape public support for hate speech laws?
Regulating hate speech is controversial, partly because partisans are assumed to disagree over which groups such laws should protect.
This article conducts a comprehensive test of how support for hate speech laws varies across partisan lines when speech targets ethnic, religious, gender, or political groups.

Based on conjoint experiments in Denmark and the United States, the results show that support for regulation increases by up to 32 percentage points when severity increases from "incivility" to "incitement to violence."

Target characteristics increase support for regulation by up to 6.3 percentage points and exert the strongest effects when speech targets ethnic and religious groups rather than gender or political groups.
These effects persist when severity is held constant and are broadly stable across severity levels.
They are also heterogeneous across partisan groups, mostly ranging from 3 to 7.2 percentage points, with one exception reaching 11.9 percentage points.
In neither country are partisans more willing to regulate hate speech targeting their political opponents than hate speech targeting their political allies.

Overall, severity has the strongest effect on support for hate speech regulation, while target characteristics have smaller, heterogeneous effects that are largest when speech targets ethnic or religious groups.
Does the target of speech shape public support for hate speech laws?

Countries around the world are introducing laws that restrict hate speech (Parekh, 2012, p. 37) directed at groups based on target characteristics such as ethnicity, religion, and gender (Sellars, 2016, p. 25).

text.text: Public opinion polls often indicate that partisans are polarized on restricting hate speech (Ekins, 2017, p. 14; Knight Foundation, 2024, p. 24; Poushter, 2015; Skaaning & Krishnarajan, 2025, p. 31).
text.formatted: Public opinion polls often indicate that partisans are polarized on restricting hate speech <ref type="bibr">(Ekins, 2017, p. 14;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Knight Foundation, 2024, p. 24;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Poushter, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Skaaning & Krishnarajan, 2025, p. 31)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, existing evidence often relies on questions that do not make it possible to distinguish whether support for hate speech restrictions depends on whom the speech targets or on how severe it is.

To make valid inferences about public opinion on restrictions of civil liberties, scholars have recommended using a concrete context instead of abstract questions (Gibson & Gouws, 2001 , pp. 1067 -71, 1074; Petersen et al., 2011, pp. 581-85).

text.text: This may be particularly important in the context of hate speech, as people can have different perceptions of what it is.

As noted by Gagliardone et al. (2016, p. 7), "hate speech continues largely to be used in everyday discourse as a generic term, mixing concrete threats to individuals' and groups' security with cases in which people may be simply venting their anger against authority."

(2016, p. 7)</ref>, "hate speech continues largely to be used in everyday discourse as a generic term, mixing concrete threats to individuals' and groups' security with cases in which people may be simply venting their anger against authority."

text.text: Thus, a central challenge in measuring support for hate speech laws is to separate the target of the speech from its severity.

Yet while hate speech laws have sparked considerable controversy (Howard, 2019, p. 94), empirical evidence on the extent to which ethnic, religious, gender, or political target characteristics shape people's support for such laws is limited.

text.text: The article addresses this shortcoming using two large conjoint experiments fielded in Denmark and the U.S., which make it possible to separate the effects of speech severity and target characteristics on support for regulating hate speech.
The design also permits an assessment of whether and to what extent specific target identities influence support for hate speech laws across partisan divides.
Moreover, it extends existing work by systematically testing the most salient target characteristics.
In short, this article conducts a comprehensive, crossnational test of how targeting people based on ethnicity, religion, gender, and political affiliation affects support for hate speech regulation.
The results show that severity and target characteristics have independent effects on support for hate speech regulation.
Support for regulation increases by up to 32 percentage points in Denmark and 31 percentage points in the U.S. when severity changes from incivility to incitement to violence.
The target of hate speech also affects support for regulation, although to a lesser degree.

On average, support for hate speech regulation increases by up to 6.3 percentage points in Denmark and the U.S. The effects of target characteristics are strongest when hate speech targets ethnic or religious groups rather than gender or political groups, and the effects are broadly stable across levels of severity.
Support for hate speech regulation also varies across partisan groups, as target characteristics have larger effects for some partisans when hate speech targets religious or ethnic minority groups.

Among partisans, target characteristics affect support for hate speech laws by 3 to 7.2 percentage points, with one exception: among left-wing respondents in Denmark, support for regulation increases by 11.9 percentage points when statements target Muslims.

Although the effects of target characteristics vary across partisans, the results also suggest substantial overlap in the extent to which target characteristics influence partisans' support for hate speech laws in the U.S. and Denmark.

The article also speaks to concerns about the adverse consequences of polarization in the U.S. Previous research shows that partisans can engage in selective censorship (Ashokkumar et al., 2020; Dias et al., 2025; Kubin et al., 2025; Lelkes & Westwood, 2016).

text.text: Similarly, general questions about banning "offensive" language without specifying context or level of severity may complicate inferences about whether people support hate speech regulation because of its severity or its target.

These challenges underscore the value of research designs that separate the effects of severity and target characteristics to yield credible inferences about public support for hate speech regulation.

This article does not provide an empirical test of whether respondents presented with generic survey questions infer different levels of severity depending on the target group; this potential mechanism is beyond its scope.
The aim is instead to separate the effects of speech severity and target characteristics on support for hate speech regulation.
Drawing on the literature, I outline three predictions about public demand for regulating hate speech.
First, the severity of the speech matters; when severity increases, people are more supportive of regulating it.
Second, the group being targeted matters; people may be willing to restrict hate speech directed at vulnerable or historically marginalized groups (e.g., racial or religious minorities).

Third, popular support for hate speech regulation may be shaped through a partisan lens, such that partisans are more supportive of regulating hate speech directed at groups they sympathize with or believe deserve protection.
I address these three accounts in turn.

text.text: To study the factors shaping support for restricting hate speech, two conjoint experiments were fielded in the U.S. and Denmark.

Conjoint experiments make it possible to disentangle the relative influence of multiple attributes (e.g., severity and target characteristics) of social media 3s on support for regulating hate speech (Bansak et al., 2021; Hainmueller et al., 2014).

text.text: The causal quantity of interest in conjoint experiments is the average marginal component effect (AMCE).

The AMCE for each attribute is the marginal effect of seeing a particular attribute level in a statement, relative to the baseline, on the preference for restricting a statement, averaged across all other possible combinations of statement attributes (Hainmueller et al., 2014).

text.text: For example, it allows researchers to estimate the average causal effect on support for hate speech regulation when the speech is directed at Muslims compared with Christians.
The conjoint experiments were fielded in two national samples in Denmark and the U.S.
The survey agency YouGov conducted 1,518 interviews in the U.S. and 1,535 interviews in Denmark between February 2 and 9, 2021.
YouGov sampled from its internet panels and employed quota sampling to match population characteristics on age, gender, region, and education.
All analyses use survey weights (see Section B in the appendix).
Respondents were excluded if they did not answer the main outcome question in any task of the conjoint experiment (147 in Denmark and 110 in the U.S.).
The final sample was 1,388 respondents in Denmark and 1,408 in the U.S. Preregistration, questionnaire, and other materials are available on the Open Science Framework: https://osf.io/7xvq6/overview.

text.text: Publics in Denmark and the U.S. generally support freedom of expression (Skaaning & Krishnarajan, 2025), but the two countries differ in two respects that are relevant to support for hate speech regulation.

text.text: First, they differ in their legal frameworks for restricting freedom of expression, including hate speech (Bleich, 2014).

text.text: Both countries restrict freedom of expression when expressions incite violence or imminent lawless action.
However, below this threshold, Danish law is more restrictive of hate speech targeting certain characteristics (see Table S4 in the appendix for an overview).

text.text: While U.S. law relies solely on the severity of the speech, Danish law is more closely aligned with the legal framework of the European Union.

For example, at the time of data collection, section 266b of the Danish Criminal Code restricted speech by which "a group of people are threatened, insulted or degraded on account of their race, skin colour, national or ethnic origin, religious belief, or because of their sexual orientation" (Justitsministeriet, 2021).

text.text: If the latter is the case, we should expect larger target effects in Denmark.
Thus, using Denmark and the U.S. as cases provides an opportunity to study the alignment between public opinion and existing laws in different legal contexts.

text.text: This study advances the extensive literature on the origins and consequences of polarization, including the relationship between polarization and partisan hostility (Amira et al., 2021; Iyengar & Westwood, 2015; Lelkes & Westwood, 2016; Westwood et al., 2022), by examining preferences for regulating hate speech against political, religious, gendered, or ethnic groups in countries with varying levels of polarization.

text.text: For instance, if polarization matters for regulating hate speech, partisans should be less (more) restrictive when hate speech targets out-group (in-group) members.
In sum, Americans likely live in a more politically polarized society with fewer restrictions on freedom of expression than Danes.
Consequently, Denmark and the U.S. provide an opportunity to assess support for hate speech regulation across distinct legal frameworks and levels of polarization.

text.text: The analysis focuses on two key attributes relevant to evaluating the hypotheses: (1) the severity of the speech and (2) the target of the statement.

text.text: Next, the target of the statement was manipulated.

Specifically, groups were included along political lines (left-wing/right-wing), religion (Christian/Muslim), ethnicity (Black/White in the U.S., Danes/immigrants in Denmark), and gender (male/female), as these are central to legal and public understandings of hate speech (Alkiviadou et al., 2020, pp. 3-12; Howard, 2019, p. 95; Siegel, 2020, pp. 56-59).

text.text: Five additional attributes were included to mimic political posts on social media and to capture potential effects based on context, message, and sender.
First, the target type was manipulated so that the statement targeted either politicians or voters.

Second, the valence of the targeted issue position (e.g., support for or opposition to affirmative action) was manipulated to make it possible to assess whether people selectively supported regulating ideas they disagreed with.
Research shows that "supporters of a political cause (e.g., abortion or gun rights) preferentially censored comments that opposed their cause" (Ashokkumar et al., 2020, p. 1).

text.text: To measure partisanship, standard measures from the American (ANES) and Danish (DNES) National Election Studies were used.

Based on answers to the question of whether participants saw themselves as supporters of a specific party, they were categorized as either Republican, Independent, or Democrat in the U.S. and either left-wing or right-wing in Denmark.
Respondents who did not report supporting or leaning toward a specific party were not included in the analyses of heterogeneous effects across partisan groups.
The Effects of Target Characteristics I begin the analysis by separating the effects of target characteristics and severity on support for hate speech laws.

To this end, I estimate the average marginal component effect (AMCE) of each target group and severity level. 5 Positive values indicate that a specific attribute level increases support for regulation (see Figure 2).

text.text: On average, support for hate speech restrictions in Denmark and the U.S. increases by 3 to 6.3 percentage points when hate speech targets religious groups (Christians and Muslims) and ethnic minorities (Black people in the U.S. and immigrants in Denmark) relative to statements that do not mention an identity group.
The largest effects of target characteristics in Denmark are observed for statements targeting Muslims, which increase support for regulation by 6.3 percentage points.
In the U.S., hate speech targeting Black people increases support by 5.4 percentage points.
In both countries, the second-largest target effects are for statements targeting Christians, which increase support for regulation by 3.5 (U.S.) and 3.4 percentage points (Denmark).
These results suggest that the public is, on average, more supportive of hate speech laws when speech targets Muslims, Christians, and ethnic minorities.
Figure 2 also displays the effects of severity.

text.text: It shows that, compared with incivility, threatening dehumanization or degradation and incitement to violence increase support for hate speech regulation by 25.3 and 32 percentage points, respectively, in Denmark and by 17.4 and 31 percentage points in the U.S. The overall pattern is that people primarily support regulating hate speech when it amounts to threats and incitement to violence, whereas they do not seem to differentiate between incivility and degradation or dehumanization that falls short of direct threats or incitement to violence.

text.text: While statistically significant effects of target characteristics are in the range of 3 to 6.3 percentage points, we might expect target characteristics to have heterogeneous effects across partisan groups and levels of severity.
In the following, I examine four plausible empirical patterns.
Are partisans more supportive of regulating hate speech targeting their political in-group or less supportive when it targets their political opponents?
The results indicate that they are not.
In Figure 2, the rows with "Democratic (Left-wing)" and "Republican (Right-wing)" provide evidence on this question.
text.formatted: In Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>, the rows with "Democratic (Left-wing)" and "Republican (Right-wing)" provide evidence on this question.

text.text: They show null effects for partisans in Denmark and the U.S. This suggests that partisans were neither more nor less likely to support hate speech regulation when it targeted their political allies or opponents than when no identity group was mentioned.

These findings contrast with research suggesting that partisans selectively accept or oppose hostility conditional on its political motivation (Kalmoe & Mason, 2022; Lelkes & Westwood, 2016; Westwood et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These findings contrast with research suggesting that partisans selectively accept or oppose hostility conditional on its political motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Kalmoe & Mason, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Lelkes & Westwood, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Westwood et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the findings provide no evidence that partisans distinguish between hate speech targeting their fellow partisans and the opposing party.
Are partisans more supportive of regulating hate speech targeting ethnic, gender, or religious groups they sympathize with?

In Denmark, the effects of target characteristics are also heterogeneous: they are more pronounced among left-wing partisans, who are more supportive of hate speech restrictions when speech targets people based on religious, ethnic, and gender characteristics.

Specifically, their support increases by 11.9 percentage points when hate speech targets Muslims, 7.2 percentage points when it targets immigrants, 5.4 percentage points when it targets women, and 5.2 percentage points when it targets Christians.
In contrast, there are no statistically significant effects of target characteristics among right-wing partisans in Denmark.
Overall, target characteristics have heterogeneous effects across partisan groups in both Denmark and the U.S.
Does the effect of target characteristics depend on the level of severity?
The results suggest that it does not.

text.text: Overall, the results suggest that severity and target characteristics have independent effects on support for hate speech regulation.
Although the effect of severity is substantially larger, the effect of target characteristics persists when severity is held constant and is largest when speech targets religious and ethnic groups.
The persistence of target effects when severity is held constant suggests that they are not wholly attributable to severity.
Moreover, partisans are neither more nor less supportive of hate speech regulation when it targets their political ingroup or out-group.
Finally, the effects of target characteristics on support for hate speech regulation are broadly similar at low and high levels of severity.

text.text: This article contributes by estimating the independent effects of severity and target characteristics on support for hate speech laws through conjoint experiments fielded in Denmark and the U.S. The results show that when severity increases from incivility to incitement to violence, support for hate speech regulation increases by up to 32 percentage points.
Target characteristics have smaller but non-zero effects that are heterogeneous across target groups and partisan groups.
These effects are broadly stable across low and high levels of severity.
In other words, the effect of target characteristics persists when the level of severity is held constant.

On average, support for hate speech regulation changes by up to 6.3 percentage points depending on the target in Denmark and the U.S. The effects are largest when hate speech targets religious groups (Christians and Muslims) and ethnic minorities (Black people in the U.S., immigrants in Denmark).
This suggests that people in Denmark and the U.S. are more supportive of regulating hate speech targeting certain groups.
There is variation across partisan groups, as the effects of target characteristics are more pronounced for some partisans when hate speech targets certain religious or ethnic minority groups.
With one exception, statistically significant effect sizes among partisans range from 3 to 7.2 percentage points.
The exception is among leftwing respondents in Denmark, whose support for regulation increases by 11.9 percentage points when statements target Muslims.
Finally, I find no evidence that partisans are more supportive of regulating hate speech targeting their political opponents than of hate speech targeting their political allies.
The findings speak to concerns about the adverse consequences of polarization among partisans (Lelkes & Westwood, 2016; Westwood et al., 2022).

text.text: In short, partisans in both countries are no more willing to regulate hate speech targeting their political opponents than to regulate hate speech targeting their political allies.

This contribution is important, as previous research suggests that partisans harbor negative feelings about their political opponents (Iyengar et al., 2012 (Iyengar et al., , 2019) ) and are more willing to tolerate and support preferential treatment of in-partisans (Lelkes & Westwood, 2016, p. 498), particularly when their partisan identity is threatened (Amira et al., 2021, pp. 473-74).

text.text: This study contributes by disentangling the effect of target characteristics from the severity of the content and estimating their independent causal impact on support for hate speech regulation.
The design manipulates different levels of severity (e.g., incivility and incitement to violence) through concrete statements (e.g., "I'm so sick of [group]!
They're a bunch of idiots who are tearing our country apart!"), which makes it possible to show that target characteristics have independent effects that are not wholly attributable to severity.
However, the design does not test whether respondents presented with generic survey questions (e.g., "offensive to [group]") infer different levels of severity depending on the target group.
Future research should test this potential mechanism by comparing generic questions with conditions in which severity is explicitly fixed.

The conjoint experiments were designed to capture a wide range of typical hate speech targets at varying levels of severity in two countries with distinct socio-political contexts, thereby enhancing the generalizability of the findings.
However, three issues warrant further investigation.

First, the experiments were designed so that each severity statement (incivility; degradation/dehumanization without threat; degradation/dehumanization with threat; incitement to violence) could apply to each target to allow for valid inferences.

Target characteristics also have smaller but non-zero effects, particularly when hate speech targets ethnic or religious groups.
These effects of target characteristics persist when severity is held constant and broadly similar across levels of severity.
In both the U.S. and Denmark, partisans differ in their overall support for hate speech regulation and, to some extent, in which target groups they are most inclined to protect.

However, it may overlook idiosyncratic forms of hate speech that might be perceived as more or less severe depending on the target group.

The study focused on typical forms of hate speech, but future research could explore these variations by considering a wider range of hate speech forms, including forms that might be uniquely severe for particular groups.
Second, the inferences drawn from the study are constrained by the specific target groups included in the experiments.

For example, it is plausible that the political right in Denmark and the U.S. might show stronger support for regulating hate speech directed at targets not represented in the experiment (e.g., national symbols such as the flag).
Future research should continue to assess citizens' support for speech restrictions across different target groups and institutional contexts.

Third, although the conjoint experiments used vignettes to mimic what people experience on social media, the design is still limited by not embedding these vignettes in real social media feeds, which may constrain the external validity of the findings.
Future research should seek to address this limitation and improve the external validity of the findings.
